## One room, two reviewers, one day

The real FDA inspection is closed out. The real AABB (Association for the Advancement of
Blood & Biotherapies) reassessment is closed out too — accreditation continued for another
two-year cycle. Both of this course's live regulatory events are, as of this morning,
history rather than open risk. Your Quality Analyst (QA) still books a full day on your
calendar anyway, and titles it, with no irony at all, "Mock Inspection / Mock Assessment."

"We got through both of the real ones," she says. "That's not the same as knowing we're
*built* to get through the next ones. I want someone who isn't us, sitting in a chair,
asking the same kinds of questions an investigator or an assessor would ask, before the
real version of either shows up again." She's already arranged it: a contracted quality
consultant, someone who has sat on both sides of this exact kind of table — real FDA
(Food and Drug Administration) inspections, real AABB on-site assessments — spends the day
at Lakeshore, playing both roles in turn. Morning session: an FDA investigator's lens.
Afternoon session: an AABB assessor's lens. Same evidence, same BECS (Blood Establishment
Computer Software) screens, same binders, two different sets of questions.

She has one more reason for picking today specifically, and she says it to you directly
before the consultant arrives. Two things have sat unresolved, referenced but never
settled, across this entire course: DED-0458's "accurate" ALCOA (Attributable, Legible,
Contemporaneously recorded, Original or a true copy, Accurate) letter, open since
`data-integrity-and-records` first ran that record through all five letters, and the
cumulative deferred-donor record's update cadence — compliant with its regulatory floor
every cycle, and still "under internal review" every time this course has mentioned it
since. "I don't want to walk into a mock session with either one still marked 'still
deciding,'" she tells you. "If we can't finish deciding something with nobody real in the
room, we're not ready for the day somebody real is." No new citations today. Just
everything this course has already built, laid out on a table, in front of someone whose
job for the day is to find the gap in it.

## Why this exercise matters — and the ITSM bridge

A mock inspection isn't a compliance checklist run a second time for luck. It's a different
kind of test entirely, and the difference is worth naming precisely. Checking that every
required document *exists* is easy — anyone can run that check with a spreadsheet. What a
mock inspection actually tests is whether Lakeshore's own account of itself holds together
under questioning: whether the 483 response, the BPDR (Biological Product Deviation Report)
filing, the AABB nonconformance closure, and the internal audit log all tell the *same*
story when a skeptical outsider pulls on each thread, or whether they quietly contradict
each other the moment someone actually compares them side by side.

You already run this exact discipline, under a different name. A **game day** or
**disaster-recovery tabletop exercise** doesn't wait for a real outage to find out whether
your runbook actually works — it stages a realistic failure on purpose, with real people
walking through real steps, specifically so the gaps surface on a Tuesday afternoon instead
of during an actual 2 a.m. incident. The value isn't the document the tabletop produces
afterward. It's what breaks, in the room, that the document never would have shown you on
its own. A mock inspection is that same exercise, aimed at a regulatory review instead of a
system outage — and it's worth running precisely *because* both real events already went
well. A program that's never been pressure-tested by someone trying to find its gaps is a
program that's never actually been tested at all; it's only ever been confirmed by people
who already knew where to look.

## The rule in plain English

**What "presenting evidence" actually means, said plainly.** It isn't handing over a stack
of documents and waiting. It's walking a reviewer through a connected story: here is the
finding, here is when it was discovered, here is who decided what, here is the record that
proves the decision was made and followed through, and here is how you'd know if it hadn't
been. Every piece of IT/BECS evidence this course has built — the 483 response, BPD-0512's
filing record, LAB-07's closed AABB nonconformance, the new Critical/Major/Minor audit
log — has to connect to the others the same way, or a reviewer will find the seam.

**What the two reviewers are actually checking, and why it's not the same check.** This
course drew this line once already, in `the-aabb-assessment-process`, and it's worth
restating here in one sentence rather than rebuilding it: an FDA-style review checks
Lakeshore's practice against binding federal regulation, using the authority
21 U.S.C. 374(a)(1) actually grants an investigator; an AABB-style review checks Lakeshore's
own policies, processes, and procedures (PPPs) against AABB's Standards, and specifically
against AABB's own stated expectation that PPPs are "followed as written," not just written.
Presenting the *same* evidence package to both lenses in one day is the fastest way to find
out whether that evidence actually supports both kinds of scrutiny, or only happens to
satisfy whichever one Lakeshore has gotten more practice with recently.

**What a "mock" review is for, specifically.** Nobody's accreditation or registration is at
stake today. That's the entire point: today is the day to actually find a weak answer, not
the day to discover one in front of a reviewer whose findings carry real consequences. A
mock session that produces zero findings isn't obviously good news — it may just mean the
exercise wasn't run hard enough to find anything.

## The actual text — reused, not re-derived

Two short phrases, already fully quoted and verified earlier in this course, carry the
weight of today's two sessions. From AABB's own "Accreditation Process" page, already
quoted in full in `the-aabb-assessment-process`:

> The expectations of an AABB assessment are that all standards are addressed in policies,
> processes and procedures (PPPs), and that PPPs are followed as written.

And FDA's own description of a written inspection report, from 21 U.S.C. 374(b)(1), already
quoted in full in `fda-inspection-authority-and-outcomes`: a report "setting forth any
conditions or practices observed by him which, in his judgment, indicate" a violation. Both
reviewers today are, in effect, rehearsing exactly those two judgments — one against federal
regulation, one against Lakeshore's own written word — against the same evidence.

## Resolving DED-0458, in front of the reviewer

The morning session is well under way when the consultant, playing the FDA role, asks your
QA to pull up a donor-eligibility determination at random and walk through how Lakeshore
knows it's trustworthy. She pulls DED-0458 — not a safer, cleaner record chosen for the
occasion, but the exact record this curriculum has been tracking since `data-integrity-and-
records` first opened it. "Four of its five ALCOA letters settled a while ago," she tells
the consultant, without hedging. "The fifth — accurate — has been open. I closed it this
week, and I want to show you exactly how."

Here's what she actually did, and it's worth sitting with, because it's the difference
between a real resolution and a convenient one. "Accurate" was never a question of whether
DED-0458 *looked* right — it looked complete from the day it was created. It was a question
of whether the record's stored determination actually matches what the donor's own
screening responses required, independently checked, not assumed because nothing had
visibly broken. So she went back to the source: the donor's actual, original screening
interview responses, the raw answers behind the determination, not the summary BECS
displays on screen. She worked through Lakeshore's own eligibility criteria against those
exact answers herself, by hand, deliberately not touching BECS's own calculation while she
did it — an independent parallel check, not a second look at the same output. Her manual
result and BECS's stored determination matched: accept. She dated and signed that
verification as its own record, now sitting alongside DED-0458 as the proof "accurate"
asked for all along.

The consultant's next question is the right one, and it's worth repeating here because it's
the whole lesson: "What would you have done if your manual check hadn't matched the
system's?" Your QA has an answer ready, because she thought it through before today, not in
the room. A mismatch would have meant quarantining that determination immediately,
escalating to you the same day, and opening a real investigation into whether the same
calculation logic affected any other donor's record — not quietly re-running the check until
it came out clean. The point isn't that today's answer was reassuring. It's that she had a
real plan for the version of today where it wasn't.

DED-0458 now passes all five ALCOA letters, each one with its own provable record, not a
single surface impression: attributable to a specific login, legible as structured BECS
data, contemporaneous once the workstation clock synchronization was verified, original as
the live BECS row rather than any printout, and now accurate, confirmed by an independent
check rather than assumed. That's the record of how a genuinely open finding gets closed —
not by deciding it was probably fine all along, but by doing the one specific thing "still
checking" was always waiting on.

## Deciding the deferred-donor cadence, out loud

The afternoon session, playing the AABB role, asks a different kind of question: what does
Lakeshore's own policy say about updating the cumulative deferred-donor record, and does
practice actually match it? This is the question `the-aabb-assessment-process` already
flagged as "discussed but deliberately left under internal review." Today, it stops being
deliberately left anywhere.

You bring the decision yourself, because it's yours to make, not your QA's. Here it is,
stated plainly, the way it needs to be logged: **Lakeshore is moving the cumulative
deferred-donor record's update cadence from the regulatory floor — at least monthly, per
606.160(e)(3) — to a fixed weekly refresh, effective immediately.** You say the next part to
the consultant exactly as directly as you need to say it to a real reviewer someday: this is
not a regulatory requirement. 606.160(e)(3) sets a floor, not a target, and Lakeshore would
be fully compliant staying at monthly. Weekly is Lakeshore's own risk-based business
decision, made because the worst-case exposure a monthly cadence leaves — a donor deferred
at one location still showing as eligible somewhere else in the system for up to just under
a month — is a real patient-safety window this organization isn't willing to carry any
longer than it has to, once the actual cost of closing most of it turned out to be
reasonable.

And you cost it honestly, the same way `data-integrity-and-records` modeled this exact
judgment call before you ever had to make it for real. Weekly means more reconciliation
runs across Brookfield, Fairview, and the central site, more staff time verifying each cycle
actually completed, and a tighter coordination window than Lakeshore's three locations have
ever run on before — real, ongoing cost, not a free settings change. You considered daily,
or a closer-to-real-time feed, and decided against it for now: the jump from weekly to daily
narrows an already-small residual window further, but at a steeper, less proportionate
increase in coordination load across three sites than the jump from monthly to weekly did.
That's not a permanent ceiling — it's today's documented balance point, open to revisiting
if Lakeshore's risk tolerance or its systems change. What makes this a real decision, and not
just a nicer-sounding number, is that it's dated, reasoned, and signed — by you — rather than
left as a sentiment everyone agreed with in a meeting and nobody wrote down.

The consultant's question back to you, playing the assessor role honestly, is the one worth
carrying forward: "Show me the record of this decision, not just today's conversation about
it." That's exactly right. A verbal commitment in a mock session is worth nothing to a real
reviewer six months from now. What goes in Lakeshore's own files today is a short, dated
decision memo: the floor (monthly), the chosen cadence (weekly), the reasoning (a bounded,
honestly-costed risk tradeoff), and the date it took effect — the same discipline this
course has used for every other judgment call that wasn't a citation.

## What both sessions actually probed

The rest of the day, stripped of the two headline resolutions, looks like this.

**The FDA-style session** pulls the 483 response file from `fda-inspection-authority-and-
outcomes` and asks whether Lakeshore's written response to both observations actually
closed them with documented corrective action, not just a promise — exactly the standard
`warning-letters-and-recalls` named as the real difference between a de-escalating response
and one that invites a Warning Letter. It pulls BPD-0512's filing record and asks for the
discovery date, the filing date, and the gap between them — confirming, without re-arguing
reportability, that the clock genuinely closed well inside 45 days. It never asks for
anything touching financial, pricing, or personnel data; your QA doesn't have to invoke the
statutory boundary today because nothing requested comes near it, the same clean outcome
module 1 modeled.

**The AABB-style session** pulls LAB-07's closed nonconformance file and asks for the dated
qualification review that closed it — present, signed, exactly where `the-aabb-assessment-
process` left it. It then pulls Lakeshore's new internal audit log and runs its own version
of the exercise `designing-an-internal-audit-program` already walked through once: LAB-07's
old gap, scored against the new Critical/Major/Minor scale, as a hypothetical Major. The
consultant doesn't treat that hypothetical as a second finding against LAB-07 — it's closed,
and stays closed — but asks a sharper question instead: "Show me a *different* finding your
new audit program actually caught, on its own, since the scale went live." Your QA has one
ready: a Minor finding from Fairview's own paper-file sampling, caught inside the new
sampling discipline's first real cycle, logged, and resolved inside its 90-day clock — proof
the program is finding things now, not just re-grading history.

## Common traps

**"A mock session that finds nothing means the program is solid."** Not necessarily, and
it's worth being honest about which conclusion a clean mock session actually supports. It
could mean the program really is solid. It could also mean the exercise wasn't pushed hard
enough, or the reviewer was handed only the evidence that was already easy to defend. A mock
inspection earns its value from how hard it tried to find something, not from the headline
number of findings it produced.

**"Closing an open finding right before a mock review looks convenient, so it's better left
open."** Wrong, and worth refuting directly, because the instinct behind it is almost
right. What actually matters isn't *when* a finding closes relative to a review — it's
whether the closure has its own dated, independent record that would hold up regardless of
when someone asked about it. DED-0458's accuracy check and the cadence decision memo both
carry their own dates and their own reasoning. A reviewer checking for a convenient,
last-minute rubber stamp finds a provable, worked verification instead. Timing a genuine
resolution to land before a scheduled review isn't suspicious; manufacturing the *appearance*
of resolution without the underlying work would be, and that's a different thing entirely.

## What this means for your job

- **Treat a mock inspection as a pressure test, not a compliance re-check.** Its whole value
  is in asking a reviewer to try to break the story your evidence tells, not in confirming
  every document still exists.
- **Never let "we passed the real one" substitute for "we've been pressure-tested since."**
  Both real events in this course went well. That's a reason to confirm the program still
  holds up under new scrutiny, not a reason to assume it automatically will next time.
- **Close an open finding only with its own dated, independent proof — never with a
  reassurance.** DED-0458's resolution is defensible because the verification record exists
  and is dated; a verbal "we checked, it's fine" would not have been.
- **When you make a risk-based decision above a regulatory floor, write down the floor, the
  choice, the reasoning, and the date — every time, not just when it's convenient.** The
  deferred-donor cadence decision is only real evidence of a mature program because it's now
  a document, not a remembered conversation.
- **Ask your QA, after any mock or real review, what the reviewer's hardest follow-up
  question was — and whether you'd want a different answer ready next time.** The consultant's
  question about what happens if DED-0458's manual check hadn't matched is exactly the kind of
  follow-up a real investigator or assessor would ask too.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA says, "Lakeshore has to update the cumulative deferred-donor record weekly now — that's the new regulatory requirement." Is she right?

No, and this is worth correcting precisely. 606.160(e)(3) still sets exactly the same floor
it always has: at least monthly. Nothing in this module changes that regulation, and nothing
could — it's federal text, not Lakeshore's to rewrite. What changed is Lakeshore's own
internal, risk-based decision to operate *above* that floor, at a weekly cadence, because the
Director weighed the residual risk of the monthly floor against the real cost of moving
faster and chose weekly. That's an internal policy choice, documented and revisable. It is
**not** a new regulatory requirement, and the two should never be described the same way to
an inspector, an assessor, or your own CIO.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: The mock reviewer asks what would have happened if the QA's independent manual check of DED-0458 hadn't matched BECS's stored determination. What's the right kind of answer?

A plan that existed *before* the check was run, not one improvised afterward: quarantine
that specific determination immediately, escalate to the Director the same day, and open an
investigation into whether the same calculation logic could have affected any other donor
record — not quietly re-running the check until it produced a cleaner result. The value of
an independent verification comes from being willing to act on a bad result, not just from
running the check in the first place.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Lakeshore's mock session produces zero new findings across both the FDA-style and AABB-style reviews. Does that prove the quality system is fully sound?

Not by itself. A clean result is consistent with a genuinely strong program, but it's also
consistent with a mock exercise that wasn't pushed hard enough, or one handed only the
evidence that was already easiest to defend. The honest question to ask afterward isn't "did
we pass" — it's "did we actually try to find something, and if we didn't, why not." A mock
inspection's value comes from the rigor of the attempt, not the number printed at the end of
it.
:::

## Where this course ends, and what's still ahead

Six modules ago, this course opened with a knock on Lakeshore's door and a question about
what an FDA investigator could and couldn't demand to see. It closes today with a contracted
consultant sitting in the same building, asking harder questions than either real reviewer
did, because nothing was actually at stake in the asking.

Here's the arc, named once, start to finish. Module 1 drew the line between FDA's real,
statutory inspection authority and the administrative vocabulary — "routine," "for-cause" —
that surrounds it, and closed with a 483 and an honest, uncertain "probably VAI" (Voluntary
Action Indicated). Module 2 sorted a real event into its right legal category — a recall, not
a market withdrawal or stock recovery — and walked FDA's own six-factor test to a reasoned
Class II recommendation, never mistaking Lakeshore's own judgment for FDA's actual
determination. Module 3 filed BPD-0512 on the one form the regulation names, to the one
office it names, well inside its 45-day clock. Module 4 put a second, entirely different
reviewer in the building — AABB's own on-site assessor — and taught the sharpest line in this
course: voluntary versus mandatory, PPP-versus-practice versus facility-versus-federal-law,
with LAB-07's own closed nonconformance as the concrete proof. Module 5 built the internal
audit program Lakeshore's debrief found missing: independence, competency, risk-based
scheduling, real sampling, and a Critical/Major/Minor grading scale with an actual clock
behind each tier. And this module put all of it in front of someone whose entire job for a
day was to find the seams — and used the occasion to finally close the two threads this
course had carried, referenced but unresolved, since its very first module.

State plainly what's resolved now, because a later course or a later session shouldn't have
to guess. **DED-0458's "accurate" ALCOA letter is closed**, by an independent, dated
verification that the stored determination matches the donor's actual screening responses —
not by assumption. **The deferred-donor-record cadence question is decided**: Lakeshore moves
from the regulatory floor (at least monthly) to a weekly cadence, by its own documented,
costed, risk-based choice, explicitly not a new regulatory requirement. **LAB-07's own
fitness-for-use gap stays exactly where module 4 left it** — closed, resolved, not reopened
by today's hypothetical re-grading exercise, which only ever existed to test the *new*
program, never to relitigate an old, settled finding.

And say plainly what stays open, because this curriculum's whole honesty convention depends
on not quietly closing things this course was never asked to touch. `data-integrity-and-
records` left two other threads unresolved on its own closing day, and neither one belonged
to this course's job: the donor-record retention-clock question (how long a *donor's*
cumulative record, spanning years of donations, actually has to be kept, distinct from
606.160(d)'s single-unit clock) is still routed to document control, not answered here. And
whether Lakeshore has ever actually set a review frequency for BECS's own audit trail — left
undecided, not wrongly defaulted, back in that course's second module — is still undecided
today. Leaving both exactly where they were left isn't an oversight. It's this curriculum
doing, on purpose, the same thing DI-0301 modeled all along: resolve what you can resolve
honestly, and say plainly what you haven't gotten to yet, rather than pretending a tidy
ending requires every thread tied off at once.

`fda-and-aabb-in-practice` is done — six modules, both of this curriculum's live reviewers
walked through in depth, and the last of `data-integrity-and-records`'s open threads that
belonged here finally closed. Three tracks remain ahead. `grc-frameworks-and-risk-management`
picks up a single risk framework — NIST's Risk Management Framework, run
categorize-through-monitor — and shows you it's the same motion as a validation release or an
internal audit cycle, spoken in one more vocabulary you'll need to be fluent in.
`healthcare-security-and-privacy` takes every donor and patient record this curriculum has
treated as a data-integrity object and finally asks its privacy question: what HIPAA (Health
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) requires, and what a breach's dual FDA-and-HIPAA
reporting duty actually looks like. `vendor-and-third-party-risk-management` turns the same
scrutiny you've just run on Lakeshore's own evidence outward, onto every vendor — BECS's own
maker included — whose systems sit underneath everything this course has covered. And
`itsm-for-regulated-blood-services`, Track 5's capstone, is where all of it — ITIL, AABB's
QSEs (Quality System Essentials), NIST's RMF, ISO 27001 — finally gets crosswalked into one
language you can speak to your CIO and your exec quality council in the same sentence,
without translating twice.

You started this course able to describe an FDA inspection and an AABB assessment as, more or
less, the same kind of visit. You end it able to sit in a room with both reviewers in one day,
hand each one a different piece of the same evidence trail, and know — because you just
proved it, not assumed it — that the story holds up either way.
